Netflix is a well-known streaming platform around the world. It has published a *What We Watched* report every six months starting in 2023 in order to provide more available and transparent information to the public. The latest report covers the first-half 2026.
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#' Acquire Netflix What We Watched Reports
#' 
#' This function will acquire and standardize all data for MP#01
#' from Netflix. Because Netflix hosts the data files behind a CDN, we
#' are accessing the release pages and automatically extracting links to the
#' relevant files (with CDN hash). 
#' 
#' After import, files are stacked vertically and some basic cleaning is
#' performed. 
load_netflix_data <- function(){
  # Note to students: Make sure you have installed the tidyverse and fs packages
  #                   before beginning this assignment. If you aren't sure,
  #                   simply run `library(tidyverse)` at your R Console and, if
  #                   you don't see an error message, `tidyverse` has been 
  #                   installed. (Same for `fs`) If you still need to install
  #                   either package, use the `install.packages` function as 
  #                   demonstrated in class.
  library(tidyverse)
  library(rvest)
  library(readxl)
  library(fs)
  
  data_dir <- path("data", "mp01")
    
  if(!dir_exists(data_dir)){
    dir_create(data_dir, showWarnings=FALSE, recurse=TRUE)
  }
  
  NETFLIX_URLS <- list(
    `2023H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-a-netflix-engagement-report",
    `2023H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2023",
    `2024H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2024",
    `2024H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2024",
    `2025H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2025",
    `2025H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2025",
    `2026H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2026"
  )
  
  download_if_needed <- function(url, local){
    if(!file_exists(local)){
      download.file(url, local, quiet = TRUE, mode = "wb")
    }
    
    return(local)
  }
    
  NETFLIX_URLS |> 
    map(read_html) |> 
    map(html_element, xpath = "//a[contains(@href, '.xlsx')]") |> 
    map_chr(html_attr, "href") |> 
    enframe("period", "url") |> 
   mutate(path = path(data_dir, paste0(period, ".xlsx")), 
          path = map2(url, path, download_if_needed), 
          data = map(path, read_excel, skip=3, na="*"), 
          data = map(data, \(x) x |> mutate(`Release Date` = as.Date(`Release Date`)))) |>
    unnest(data) |> 
    select(-url, -path) |> 
    mutate(year=str_sub(period, 1, 4), 
           half=str_sub(period, start=6), 
           period_start = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 1, 7), 1), 
           period_end = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 7, 12), if_else(half==1, 30, 31))) |> 
    filter(!is.na(`Hours Viewed`)) |> 
    mutate(live_event = !is.na(Runtime) & str_detect(Runtime, "\\d+:\\d+\\*"), 
           clean_time = str_remove(Runtime, fixed("*")),
           Runtime = 60 * hour(hm(clean_time)) + minute(hm(clean_time))) |>
    select(-clean_time) |>
    mutate(Runtime = coalesce(Runtime, mean(Runtime, na.rm=TRUE)), 
           .by=Title, 
           Title = stringi::stri_trans_general(Title, "Latin-ASCII"),
           Title = str_remove(Title, " // .*"), 
           Title = str_remove(Title, "[^[:ascii:]].*"), 
           Title = str_trim(Title)) |>
    filter_out(Title == "") |>
    select(year, 
           period, 
           period_start, 
           period_end, 
           Title, 
           -half, 
           Runtime, 
           Views, 
           `Hours Viewed`, 
           `Release Date`,
           `Available Globally?`, 
           live_event)
}

NETFLIX_DATA <- load_netflix_data()
```

To make data set look more readable and easier to manipulate, we use `rename` to get nice tidy column names. Then, we examine and describe the data set by using `glimps()` and `skimr` package.

## Data Introduction
`NETFLIX_DATA` has 61,892 rows and 11 columns. It contains four types of variables, which are *character*, *Date*, *logical*, and *numeric*.
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
NETFLIX_DATA <- load_netflix_data() |>
  rename(
    title = Title,
    runtime = Runtime,
    views = Views,
    hours_viewed = `Hours Viewed`,
    release_date = `Release Date`,
    available_globally = `Available Globally?`
  ) |>
  mutate(
    year = as.integer(year),
    available_globally = (available_globally == "Yes")
  )
```

## Missing Data
The summary shows that there are **four** variables in `NETFLIX_DATA` contain missing values. `release_date` has the highest amount of missing data (35,251 entries), followed by `views` (18,198), `runtime` (13,085), and `available_globally` (2).
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(skimr)
glimpse(NETFLIX_DATA)
skim(NETFLIX_DATA)
```

## Exploratory Questions
### Inline Value Questions
We explore several interesting questions to analyze the data:


1. What date range is covered by this data set?
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(scales)

date_max <- max(NETFLIX_DATA$period_end)
date_min <- min(NETFLIX_DATA$period_start)
```
By using `min()` and `max()` on the period start and end dates, we found that the date range is from **`r date_min`** to **`r date_max`**.

2. How many different shows and movies are covered in this data set?
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
n_title <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  distinct(title) |>
  nrow()
num_title <- comma(n_title)
```
To count the number of the shows and movies, we use `distinct()` to make sure that each show and movie has only one record. Therefore, we can get the result that there are **`r num_title`** different shows and movies in this data set. 

3. How many total hours have been spent watching shows from the Bridgerton universe?
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
hours <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(str_detect(title, "Bridgerton")) |>
  summarize(total = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pull(total)
```
After filtering the titles by `filter()` and summing the `hours_viewed`, the total viewing time for shows from the *Bridgerton universe* is **`r scales::comma(hours)`** hours.
  
4. How many total hours have been spent watching the five seasons of Stranger Things?
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
st_hours <- NETFLIX_DATA  |>
  filter(str_detect(title, "Stranger Things"))  |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Beyond|Tales|Fireplace"))  |>
  summarize(total = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE))  |>
  pull(total)
```
Similar to the previous question, we use `filter()` and `summarize()` to find out the answer. The difference is that before calculating the total hours, we use `filter_out()` to *exclude* the behind-the-scenes show, the animated spin-off, and the background music. The total hours for watching the five seasons of Stranger Things is **`r scales::comma(st_hours)`** hours.
  
5. What percentage of total watch time was spent on the Top 10 titles of 2026H1?
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
view_time_2026 <- NETFLIX_DATA  |>
  filter(period == "2026H1")
thour_2026 <- sum(view_time_2026$hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)
top_2026 <- view_time_2026  |>
  slice_max(hours_viewed, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE)  |>
  summarize(hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE))  |>
  pull(hours)
per_time <- top_2026 / thour_2026
percent_time <- percent(per_time, accuracy=0.01)
```
We first use `filter()` to select the data in the first half of 2026. Then, we use ` slice_max()` to get the Top 10 titles and `sum()` to calculate the total hours for 2026H1 and Top 10 titles. We discovered that the percentage of total watch time spent on the Top 10 titles of 2026H1 is **`r percent_time`**.
  
6. What fraction of Netflix’s catalog is globally available?
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
global_share <- NETFLIX_DATA  |>
  summarize(title_share = sum(available_globally == TRUE, na.rm = TRUE) / n(), hours_share = sum(hours_viewed[available_globally], na.rm = TRUE) / sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE))
global_title_pct <- percent(global_share$title_share, accuracy=0.01)
global_hours_pct <- percent(global_share$hours_share, accuracy=0.01)
```
By using `summarize()` to calculate the share of globally available titles and their share of total viewing hours after removing missing data, it shows that there are **`r global_title_pct`** of shows and movies are globally available, and these titles account for **`r global_hours_pct`** of the total viewing hours in this data set.
  
### Further Questions
To get a much closer look at the data, we use Tables to answer further questions that we found in this data set:

1. What was the top title (by total hours viewed) in each period and what fraction of total viewership did it capture?
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(gt)

table1_data <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period) |>
  mutate(total_period_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  slice_max(order_by = hours_viewed, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  mutate(share = hours_viewed / total_period_hours) |>
  select(period, title, hours_viewed, share) |>
  ungroup()

table1_data |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Top Netflix Title by Period",
    subtitle = "Leading title and share of aggregate watch time per 6-month window"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    period = "Period",
    title = "Top Title",
    hours_viewed = "Hours Viewed",
    share = "Fraction of total viewership"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(columns = hours_viewed, decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = share, decimals = 2)
```
To calculate the percentage for each period, we grouped the data by `period`, used `mutate()` to create a new column for total viewed hours within each period, and used `slice_max()` to identify the title with the highest viewership.

The fraction of total viewership was calculated by dividing the Top title’s hours viewed by the total hours viewed in the same period. As shown in the table, the top title captured only around 0.87% to 1.35% of total viewing time in each period, and *Squid Game: Season 2* was the only one that ranked at the Top in two consecutive periods. 

2. How has Netflix’s catalog changed in size over the periods for which we have questions?
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
catalog_evolution <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarize(
    total_titles = n_distinct(title),
    total_runtime_hours = sum(runtime, na.rm = TRUE) / 60
  ) |>
  ungroup()

catalog_evolution |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Netflix Catalog Size Changed by Period",
    subtitle = "Number of unique titles and cumulative runtime per 6-month period"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    period = "Period",
    total_titles = "Total Titles",
    total_runtime_hours = "Total Runtime (Hours)"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(total_titles, total_runtime_hours), decimals = 0)
```
To examine how Netflix's catalog changed over time, we grouped the data by `period` and used `summarize()` to compute `n_distinct(title)` (the number of unique titles) and `runtime` (the total catalog runtime converted into hours).

The table shows an unusual pattern in 2023H1: it had *the largest number of unique titles* but *the lowest total catalog runtime*. From 2023H2 to 2026H1, however, both the number of titles and total runtime **increased steadily**. The catalog grew from 6,574 titles and 50,117 hours in 2023H2 to 8,163 titles and 62,855 hours in 2026H1, which means that Netflix generally expanded over time in *both* the number of available titles and the total amount of catalog runtime. 

3. Which titles have had the most consistently high viewership across all periods?
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
n_periods <- n_distinct(NETFLIX_DATA$period)

staple_titles <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(title) |>
  summarize(
    periods_present = n_distinct(period),
    avg_hours = mean(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_hours = sd(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  filter(periods_present == n_periods) |>
  mutate(cv = sd_hours / avg_hours) |>
  filter(avg_hours >= quantile(avg_hours, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(cv) |>
  slice_head(n = 8)

staple_titles |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Top Consistent Titles Across Periods",
    subtitle = "Titles maintaining steady high viewership across all reporting periods"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    title = "Title",
    avg_hours = "Avg. Hours Viewed",
    sd_hours = "Std. Deviation",
    cv = "Coefficient of Variation"
  ) |>
  cols_hide(columns = periods_present) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(avg_hours, sd_hours), decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = cv, decimals = 1)
```
There are `r n_periods` in Netflix's data set. To identify titles with consistently high viewership across all periods, we used `summarize()` to calculate the number of periods in which each title appeared and `filter()` to keep only titles that appeared in every period. We also computed each title's average viewing hours (`avg_hours`) and standard deviation (`sd_hours`). As we known, the lower `cv` means more stable of the viewership, so we divided `sd_hours`by `avg_hours` to calculate coefficient of variation (`cv`).

After selecting the top 25% titles based on average viewing hours and ranking the stability by `arange(cv)`, the result shows that the several seasons of *Superstore* have low `cv`, ranging from 4.3%~5.4%, indicating relatively stable viewership across periods. *The Seven Deadly Sins* has the highest `avg_hours` among this table, but it is less stable than than the *Superstore* seasons and *BoJack Horseman: Season 1*.

4. Within each period, what fraction of time was spent on ‘shows’ vs movies?
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
show_movie_share <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(
    content_type = case_when(
      str_detect(title, regex("season|series", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Show",
      runtime > 240 ~ "Show",
      !is.na(runtime) ~ "Movie",
      TRUE ~ "Unknown"
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(period, content_type) |>
  summarize(total_hours_viewed = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  group_by(period) |>
  mutate(share = total_hours_viewed / sum(total_hours_viewed)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(period, content_type, share) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = content_type, values_from = share, values_fill = 0)

show_movie_share |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Share of Viewing Time: Shows vs. Movies",
    subtitle = "Classified by title keywords or runtime exceeding 240 minutes"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    period = "Period",
    Show = "Shows",
    Movie = "Movies"
  ) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = where(is.numeric), decimals = 1)
```
Unfortunately, our data does not clearly delineate shows from movies. To separate all titles into two categories, we classified a title as a show if its runtime was over 4 hours (240 minutes) or if the title contained the word “Season” or "Series". We then summed the total viewing hours for shows and movies within each period and divided each category's viewing hours by the total viewing hours in that period to calculate its fraction of viewing time. It is worth noting that, **some titles miss the data of runtime and without the word "Season" or "Series"**. This problem is more obvious during 2023H1. In order not to separate those titles into wrong categories, we set another `content_type` called **Unknown**.

As we can see, except for 2023H1, which has a relatively high proportion of *Unknown*, the fraction of *Unknown* is below 2% in other periods. Looking closer at the result of Movies and Shows, we can see that most viewing time was classified as Shows. Even though 2023H1 has a relatively low combined share of viewing time classified as Shows or Movies, the share of Shows is still much higher than that of Movies. From 2023H2 to 2026H1, the share of viewing time for Shows ranges from **96.1%** to **97.6%**, showing relatively little variation across periods.

5. How does the performance of live events compare to pre-taped content? Does the average live event draw more viewership than an average piece of pre-taped content? How about a ‘top tier’ live event vs ‘top tier’ pre-taped content?
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
live_vs_pretaped <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(performance_type = if_else(live_event, "Live Event", "Pre-taped Content")) |>
  group_by(performance_type) |>
  summarize(
    count = n(),
    avg_hours = mean(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_hours = median(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    top_tier_avg = mean(hours_viewed[hours_viewed >= quantile(hours_viewed, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE)], na.rm = TRUE)
  )

live_vs_pretaped |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Performance: Live Events vs. Pre-taped Content",
    subtitle = "Comparison of average, median, and top 5% viewership"
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    performance_type = "Performance Format",
    count = "Title Count",
    avg_hours = "Mean Hours",
    median_hours = "Median Hours",
    top_tier_avg = "Top 5% Mean Hours"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(count, avg_hours, median_hours, top_tier_avg), decimals = 0)
```
To compare live events with pre-taped content, we separated titles into two groups based on the `live_event` variable. Then, we calculated the number of titles (`count`), average viewing hours (`avg_hours`), and median viewing hours (`median_hours`) for each group. We also defined the **top 5% of titles** as top-tier content (`top_tier_avg`) and calculated their average viewing hours to compare the performance of the best-performing content in each group.

The result shows that **pre-taped content generally has better viewing performance than live events**. The average viewing hours of live events are about 3.56 million hours, compared with about 8.29 million hours for pre-taped content. However, the median viewing hours of these two content types are very similar, and the difference between mean and median is much greater in  pre-taped content. This huge gap can partly be explained by `top_tier_avg`. For the top 5% of content, the average viewing hours are about 26.1 million for top-tier live events and 80.4 million for top-tier pre-taped content, indicating that some highly viewed pre-taped titles may increase its average.

## Platform Strategy Memo
```{r}
# Big hits
library(dplyr)
big_hit_range <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  group_by(period) |>
  mutate(total_period_hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  slice_max(order_by = hours_viewed, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  mutate(share = hours_viewed / total_period_hours) |>
  summarize(min_top_share = min(share), max_top_share = max(share)) |>
  ungroup()

min_top_share <- min(big_hit_range$min_top_share, na.rm = TRUE)
max_top_share <- max(big_hit_range$max_top_share, na.rm = TRUE)

library(scales)
per_min <- percent(min_top_share, accuracy = 0.01)
per_max <- percent(max_top_share, accuracy = 0.01)

# Shows vs Movies
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)

show_movie_share <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(
    content_type = case_when(
      str_detect(title, regex("season|series", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Show",
      runtime > 240 ~ "Show",
      !is.na(runtime) ~ "Movie",
      TRUE ~ "Unknown"
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(period, content_type) |>
  summarize(total_hours_viewed = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop_last") |>
  mutate(share = total_hours_viewed / sum(total_hours_viewed)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(period, content_type, share) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = content_type, values_from = share, values_fill = 0)

show_range <- show_movie_share |>
  filter(period != "2023H1") |>
  summarize(
    min_show_share = min(Show, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_show_share = max(Show, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

min_show_val <- show_range$min_show_share
max_show_val <- show_range$max_show_share

per_min_show <- percent(min_show_val, accuracy = 0.01)
per_max_show <- percent(max_show_val, accuracy = 0.01)

remain_val   <- 1 - min_show_val
remain_share <- percent(remain_val, accuracy = 0.01)

# Live vs Pre-taped
live_vs_pretaped <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(performance_type = if_else(live_event, "Live Event", "Pre-taped Content")) |>
  group_by(performance_type) |>
  summarize(
    count = n(),
    avg_hours = mean(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_hours = median(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    top_tier_avg = mean(hours_viewed[hours_viewed >= quantile(hours_viewed, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE)], na.rm = TRUE)
  )

live_value <- live_vs_pretaped |>
  filter(performance_type == "Live Event") |>
  select(avg_hours, median_hours)

pretaped_value <- live_vs_pretaped |>
  filter(performance_type == "Pre-taped Content") |>
  select(avg_hours, median_hours)
```
### Suggestions for Netflix's future develop path
To provide useful and specific suggestions for Netflix's content strategy in 2027 and further periods, we **analyzed the data set from 2023H1 to 2026H1**. Based on the viewing data across the entire data period, we recommend that Netflix keep focusing on shows and maintain diverse content catalog instead of putting too much resources into a small number of big-hit works. In addition, pre-taped content would be better to be regarded as a main-focused part in their strategy.

First of all, Netflix should not only focus on a few big-hit shows or movies. Although there is the most popular title with the highest viewing hours in each period, the top title **only accounts for `r per_min` to `r per_max` of total viewing hours**, which is a small fraction of total viewership. It also means that the remaining titles still contribute the majority of viewing hours. Therefore, we suggest that Netflix should put more effort on **maintaining a diverse catalog**, especially those evergreen works, while promoting big-hit shows or movies in the future. By doing so, it can attract and cater to more viewers with different preference and increase the total viewing hours.

Comparing shows and movies, we also recommend that Netflix should pay more attention to shows, such as seasons or series. Despite of the limitation of the data set, we cannot obtain sufficient information to classify all titles into two category accurately, especially in *2023H1*, which has more missing runtime data. To reduce the influence of this problem, we excluded 2023H1 from this comparison and used keywords of title and runtime to categorize the remaining titles. We noticed that **the category of *Show* accounts for `r per_min_show` to `r per_max_show` of total viewing time**, which is a very high percentage. The remain percentage, including *Movies* and *Unknown*, is no more than `r remain_share`, and this trend is relatively stable across periods. This result shows that viewers tend to spend much more time on show under our classification. Therefore, Netflix should **continue investing in shows**, especially series that can continue for multiple seasons.

Last but not least, the live events may be more suitable as a complementary part of Netflix's content strategy. The average viewing hours of live events are about `r round(live_value$avg_hours / 1e6, 2)` million hours, compared with about `r round(pretaped_value$avg_hours / 1e6, 2)` million hours for pre-taped content. However, the median viewing hours of these two content types are very similar, and the difference between mean and median is much greater in  pre-taped content. This huge gap may be caused by **some highly viewed pre-taped titles among the data set**, which pull up the overall average of pre-taped content. This is an important sign for Netflix while designing their future strategy. Even though both content types are important, we still suggest Netflix to **continue prioritizing pre-taped content** while using live events as a complementary option.

To sum up, Netflix's future strategy should balance strong-performing content with a diverse catalog. No matter what type of content it is, the company should not rely heavily on a small groups of content that have relatively high viewing hours. For more sustainable and consistent growth, it would be better for the company to maintain a variety of content types to attract different groups of viewers.
